There is a real difference. `structuredClone` keeps Dates as Dates and handles Map, Set, undefined values and circular references, while the JSON round trip turns Dates into strings, drops undefined and functions, and throws on circular references. The JSON trick only makes sense when you deliberately want a JSON-safe copy, and `structuredClone` throws on functions and DOM nodes.

Both run TypeScript without a separate build step, but tsx transpiles with esbuild and does no type checking, which makes it fast and much better with ESM and mixed module setups. ts-node uses the TypeScript compiler and type-checks by default unless you turn on transpile-only, which is slower and often needs more config for ESM. So with tsx you still want `tsc --noEmit` somewhere to catch type errors.
Action: Nothing to change; just keep a typecheck step in place for the scripts.

`docker compose up -d` creates any missing containers, networks and volumes, recreates containers whose config or image changed, and starts everything detached. `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and are stopped, with no creation and no picking up of compose file changes. So use `up -d` normally, and `start` to resume stopped containers as they were.

A 403 CSRF failure after moving a form into a partial usually means the token is not reaching the htmx request. Common causes: the partial is rendered without the request (so `{% csrf_token %}` outputs nothing), the `{% csrf_token %}` tag was left outside the moved form, or the token was sent via an `hx-headers` attribute on an element that is no longer an ancestor of the form. A token in the base template only helps if the form or one of its parents carries it.
Action: Ask you to share the partial and the view that renders it, so I can check where the token ends up.
